items.name: Geology -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
J Harlen Bretz proposed in the 1920s that the Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington were carved by catastrophic flooding. Critics of Bretz argued that the coulees were cut by slow stream erosion acting over millions of years. The adjudication turned on whether the forms of the scabland tract—dry cataracts, hanging coulees, scoured rock basins and house-sized erratics—required a discharge that no ordinary river could supply. Bretz published "The Channeled Scabland of the Columbia Plateau" in 1923, and the organized response from the profession came only after that paper was in print.

That members of the Geological Society of Washington attacked Bretz's hypothesis at a 1927 meeting shows how completely the doctrine of uniformitarianism dominated geological thinking at the time he advanced it. Although that gradualist orthodoxy held the field, Bretz pressed the case that a single deluge had stripped the basalt plateau; and it was that same orthodoxy that drove his colleagues to insist on the patient work of ordinary streams over millions of years as the agent that cut the coulees. After that meeting, Bretz formally retracted his flood hypothesis in 1930 and adopted the gradual-erosion explanation.

Bretz named the event the Spokane Flood. Joseph Thomas Pardee identified Glacial Lake Missoula as the source of the floodwater. Pardee traced the floodwaters to Pleistocene Lake Bonneville in Utah, an identification that cannot be squared with an origin for the water in the ice-dammed basin of western Montana. Pardee documented giant current ripples on the Camas Prairie in western Montana, gravel dunes with wavelengths measured in hundreds of feet whose very existence shows that the failure of an ice dam released the water that swept across the scablands.

At least one of two things must then be true of that drainage, and perhaps both: an ice dam gave way and loosed the water it had held, or the water escaped from the impounded lake on more than one occasion. The rhythmically bedded deposits of the Touchet Formation record dozens of separate flood events. The last of the Missoula floods occurred roughly 15,000 years ago. It is the Touchet rhythmite stratigraphy, more than any other line of field evidence, that establishes the repeated emptying of the impounded lake rather than a single release. Measurements of discharge, the hydraulic interpretation of the Montana dune fields and the layered valley fills of the lower Columbia system thus together carried the question of mechanism out of the realm of doctrine and into that of measurable sedimentary record.
